items.followUp: Why is the value of g different at the poles and at the equator?

rubric.why: The Earth’s shape causes its radius, and therefore distance from its centre, to vary from place to place.
rubric.description: Relates variation in g to Earth’s shape or radius.
rubric.how: Award for stating that Earth is not a perfect sphere, so the distance from its centre differs at different places.

rubric.why: The variation has observable effects: g is greater at the poles than at the equator and also changes with altitude and depth.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example or consequence of g varying from place to place.
rubric.how: Award for a correct comparison or for mentioning variation with altitude, depth, or latitude.

modelAnswer: The value of g varies from place to place because the Earth is not a perfect sphere; its radius is greater at the equator than at the poles.
Therefore, g is smaller at the equator and greater at the poles; it also changes with altitude and depth.

items.followUp: How can the kinetic energy of wind be converted into electrical energy?

rubric.why: Wind is moving air and therefore possesses kinetic energy.
rubric.description: Identifies wind or moving air as the energy source.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the kinetic energy of moving air.

rubric.why: Wind turns a turbine or windmill, which can drive a generator to produce electricity.
rubric.description: Explains how wind energy is made useful.
rubric.how: Award for describing the use of a windmill or turbine to generate electricity.

modelAnswer: Moving air, called wind, possesses kinetic energy.
Wind turns the blades of a wind turbine, which drives a generator to produce electrical energy.

items.followUp: State Hooke’s law and write the relation between force and extension.

rubric.why: Hooke’s law applies only while the material remains within its elastic limit.
rubric.description: States the condition under which Hooke’s law holds.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning the elastic limit.

accept: extension is directly proportional to force
force is directly proportional to extension
rubric.why: The defining relationship is that extension varies directly with the applied force.
rubric.description: States the proportionality or its mathematical form.
rubric.how: Award for the direct proportionality or a correct equation such as F = kx.

modelAnswer: Within the elastic limit, the extension produced in a body is directly proportional to the applied force.
F ∝ x, or F = kx, where x is the extension and k is the spring constant.

items.followUp: Define Young’s modulus and write its formula in terms of force, area, length and extension.

accept: ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain
tensile stress divided by tensile strain
rubric.why: Young’s modulus is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain.
rubric.description: Gives the definition of Young’s modulus.
rubric.how: Award for stating the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain.

rubric.why: The formula follows from stress = F/A and strain = ΔL/L.
rubric.description: Writes the mathematical form of Young’s modulus.
rubric.how: Award for the stress-to-strain formula or its expanded equivalent.

modelAnswer: Young’s modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit.
Y = tensile stress / tensile strain.
Y = (F/A) / (ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL).

items.followUp: A force acting on a 4 kg body produces an acceleration of 12 m/s². What acceleration will the same force produce in a 6 kg body?

rubric.why: The first body’s mass must be identified from the question.
rubric.description: Records the first body’s mass.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the mass as 5 kg.

rubric.why: The first acceleration is needed to calculate the force.
rubric.description: Records the first acceleration.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the acceleration as 10 m/s².

rubric.why: Newton’s second law gives the force acting on both bodies.
rubric.description: Calculates the force from the first body.
rubric.how: Award for using F = ma and obtaining 50 N.

rubric.why: The same force acts on the second body, so its acceleration is force divided by its mass.
rubric.description: Finds the acceleration of the 8 kg body with the correct unit.
rubric.how: Award for substituting into a = F/m and giving 6.25 m/s²; award one mark for the correct setup if the final calculation is wrong.

modelAnswer: Given: m₁ = 5 kg, a₁ = 10 m/s², m₂ = 8 kg.
Force on the first body: F = m₁a₁.
F = 5 kg × 10 m/s² = 50 N.
For the second body: a₂ = F/m₂.
a₂ = 50 N / 8 kg = 6.25 m/s².
The acceleration produced is 6.25 m/s².

items.followUp: Describe translatory, rotatory and vibratory motion, giving an example of each.

rubric.why: Translatory motion includes linear, circular and random motion, in which the body moves from one place to another.
rubric.description: Describes translatory motion and its forms.
rubric.how: Award for explaining translatory motion and identifying its forms or giving a correct form with its description.

rubric.why: In rotatory motion, a body turns about an axis.
rubric.description: Describes rotatory motion.
rubric.how: Award for identifying rotation about a fixed axis.

rubric.why: Vibratory motion is a repeated to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
rubric.description: Describes vibratory motion.
rubric.how: Award for explaining the to-and-fro motion about a mean position.

modelAnswer: Translatory motion: A body moves from one place to another; all its particles move through the same distance in the same direction in a given time.
Linear motion is along a straight line, circular motion is along a circular path, and random motion is along an irregular path.
Rotatory motion: A body turns about a fixed axis; its particles move in circular paths around the axis.
Vibratory motion: A body moves repeatedly to and fro about its mean position.

items.followUp: A vehicle has a weight of 15 kN and a speed of 12 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy. Take g = 10 m/s².

rubric.why: The given weight must be converted to newtons for use in SI calculations.
rubric.description: Records or converts the weight correctly.
rubric.how: Award for stating 12 kN = 12000 N.

rubric.why: Kinetic energy requires mass, which is found from weight using W = mg.
rubric.description: Finds the car’s mass using its weight.
rubric.how: Award for using m = W/g and obtaining 1200 kg, taking g = 10 m/s².

rubric.why: This is the formula for kinetic energy.
rubric.description: Writes the correct kinetic-energy formula.
rubric.how: Award for stating KE = ½mv².

rubric.why: Substitution of the mass and speed gives the kinetic energy; using g = 9.8 m/s² instead gives an equivalent value close to 244.9 kJ.
rubric.description: Substitutes and calculates kinetic energy with a correct unit.
rubric.how: Award for a correct substitution and final answer. Accept 240 kJ using g = 10 m/s² or approximately 244.9 kJ using g = 9.8 m/s².

modelAnswer: Given: W = 12 kN = 12000 N, v = 20 m/s, g = 10 m/s².
Mass: m = W/g.
Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv².
The kinetic energy of the car is 240000 J, or 240 kJ.

items.followUp: State the two conditions for equilibrium of a body and explain what each condition means.

rubric.why: A body is in equilibrium only when both translational and rotational equilibrium conditions are satisfied.
rubric.description: Identifies that two conditions are required.
rubric.how: Award for stating that there are two conditions for equilibrium.

rubric.why: Zero resultant force prevents linear acceleration and gives translational equilibrium.
rubric.description: States the first condition: zero resultant force.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the resultant force on the body is zero.

rubric.why: Zero resultant torque prevents angular acceleration and gives rotational equilibrium.
rubric.description: States the second condition: zero resultant torque.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the resultant torque about any point is zero.

rubric.why: Explaining the consequences shows the meaning of the two equilibrium conditions.
rubric.description: Explains what the conditions imply for the body.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the body has no linear and no angular acceleration.

modelAnswer: Two conditions are needed for a body to be in equilibrium.
First condition: The resultant force on the body must be zero (ΣF = 0), so there is no linear acceleration.
Second condition: The resultant torque on the body must be zero (Στ = 0), so there is no angular acceleration.
Thus, the body is in both translational and rotational equilibrium.
